turns.name: P1-intro
turns.question: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?

card.problem: Tell the project that best shows mobile skills: users, problem, responsibility
card.adopted: none
card.heard: pick the project, who used it, problem, my responsibility
card.say: The project that best shows my mobile skills is the AI trip planner at KKday. Our users were travelers on the KKday app, mostly in Asia. They wanted to book tours and activities at their destination. Planning by hand was slow: they had to work out the budget, search products one by one, and put the plan together. So we let them type something like "Tokyo, RMB 5,000, three days", and the AI gave them a plan they could book. My responsibility started at the technical plan and the agent design. I also built the core backend and wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan. It ended at the product and order tools, which other teams owned, and at the app screens, which the app team built with me. The chat gives no reliable amount, so the user types the amount on that confirm screen; the model never fills it in. The server binds that authorization to the payer, recipient, amount and expiry; chat or model text can suggest a payment but never authorizes one. If the model calls the payment tool again, that call maps to the same intent and client ID, so it can never create a second transfer.
card.then: Next, I'll cover how the plan reached the phone and what happened when a plan failed our checks.

updates: The plan reached the phone as a stream, so the first day card showed while the rest was still being made. Before anything reached the user, the backend checked the structure, the product IDs and the location limits. If a check failed, it retried with the exact error, and after the retry limit it fell back to a safe default. The server binds that authorization to the payer, recipient, amount and expiry; chat or model text can suggest a payment but never authorizes one. If the model calls the payment tool again, that call maps to the same intent and client ID, so it can never create a second transfer.

card.say: On reopen, A sees the transfer as "still checking", not success and not failure. The ViewModel reads the open intent from the local database and asks the server for that client ID. If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight. I'd resend that same client ID only while the server's idempotency window still covers it; after that, I'd rely on the lookup and reconciliation, never a new ID.

Candidate: Our users were travelers on the KKday app, mostly in Asia.
Candidate: They wanted to book tours and activities at their destination.
Candidate: Planning by hand was slow: they had to work out the budget, search products one by one, and put the plan together.
Candidate: So we let them type something like "Tokyo, RMB 5,000, three days", and the AI gave them a plan they could book.
Candidate: My responsibility started at the technical plan and the agent design.
Candidate: I also built the core backend and wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan.
Candidate: It ended at the product and order tools, which other teams owned, and at the app screens, which the app team built with me.

Candidate: The plan reached the phone as a stream, so the first day card showed while the rest was still being made.
Candidate: Before anything reached the user, the backend checked the structure, the product IDs and the location limits.
Candidate: If a check failed, it retried with the exact error, and after the retry limit it fell back to a safe default.

Interviewer: On the KKday AI trip planner, you said you built the core backend and the Android code that reads the streamed plan — which exact pieces of that did you write yourself versus the app team?
Candidate: I wrote the agent design and the core backend myself.

Candidate: I also agreed the response format with the app team: the day cards, product cards and map points.
Candidate: The app team built the screens around it, and the product and order tools stayed with their own teams.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: I'll take the day card.
Candidate: The user sends "Tokyo, RMB 5,000, three days", and the backend streams the plan back.
Candidate: On Android, my code reads the SSE stream and turns each day card into UI state.
Candidate: The screens around it were the app team's work, but the stream reading and the card state were mine.
Candidate: The parser runs on Dispatchers.IO, not the main thread.
Candidate: Each day card updates a StateFlow, so the UI only redraws the card that changed.
Candidate: If the stream drops, I keep the cards already shown and mark the rest as pending.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest bug was a day card that sometimes showed half a price.
Candidate: It only happened on slow networks, so I couldn't make it happen on my phone.
Candidate: At first I suspected the backend was sending bad data.
Candidate: Then I logged the raw stream on a slow network and saw one card split across two chunks.
Candidate: My parser read each chunk as a full card, so the last field was cut off.
Candidate: That log proved me wrong, and I fixed it by buffering until the closing brace arrived.

Interviewer: You said buffering until the closing brace fixed it — how did you confirm that was the actual root cause and not just masking the symptom, and what did you see in production after shipping it?
Candidate: I confirmed it by replaying the same slow network with the raw stream logged.

Candidate: I had two other options.

Candidate: I didn't pick the backend change because it needed a server release, and the app fix could ship in our own release.
Candidate: After release, I watched our error reports for incomplete cards.
Candidate: Its limit is that it only covers the cases we saw, so it can't prove there's no problem on devices or networks we didn't test.
